claims.text: A procedural justice framework in algorithmic decision-making can be established using procedural justice theory.
Standards clarity alone does not increase perceived fairness in algorithmic allocations.
Outcome explanation produces mixed effects on perceived fairness, increasing it in some contexts and decreasing it in others.
Outcome explanation reduces perceived algorithmic accountability.
Outcome control consistently improves perceived fairness in algorithmic goods division.
Outcome control improves perceived fairness by enabling users to recognize algorithmic limitations and reallocate goods to fit their specific contexts.

evidence.description: The paper proposes a procedural justice framework drawing from procedural justice theory to identify elements that promote fairness perceptions.
Findings from the within-subjects laboratory study suggested that standards clarity alone did not increase perceived fairness.
Outcome explanation had mixed effects, increasing or decreasing perceived fairness.
Outcome explanation reduced algorithmic accountability in the laboratory study.
Outcome control universally improved perceived fairness across participants.
Outcome control improved fairness by allowing people to realize the inherent limitations of decisions and redistribute goods to better fit their contexts.

methodologies.name: Within-subjects laboratory evaluation of procedural justice interface
methodologies.description: Built an interactive interface implementing standards clarity, outcome explanation, and group outcome control, and evaluated user perceptions in a goods division domain.
